The book effectively bridges the gap between agricultural production and agribusiness management by demonstrating how value addition can serve as a catalyst for wealth creation, food security, rural industrialization, and youth empowerment. One of the most commendable features of the book is its multidisciplinary approach. It integrates concepts from entrepreneurship, agro - processing technology, capacity management, financial planning , risk management, value - chain development, and export logistics into a coherent framework that is both educational and operational. Rather than merely presenting theoretical discussions, the author provides practical tools, case studies, assessment exercises, flashcards, and real - world examples that support experiential learning and business application. The book is particularly valuable for farmers, agripreneurs, agro - processors, agricultural students, cooperative societies, entrepreneurship trainers, dev elopment practitioners, financial institutions, policymakers, and investors seeking opportunities within agricultural value chains. Its emphasis on rural youth empowerment and local enterprise development also makes it a significant contribution to sustainable community development and employment generation. Overall, this publication successfully transforms agricultural entrepreneurship from an abstract concept into a practical pathway for economic development. It deserves recognition as a useful handbook, training guide, and reference material for agribusiness education and professional development. I n the first place, the factory operations tend to provide cash flow to farmers to finance their farm production just as it enables the urban and rural consumers and industrial users to have access to intermediate or semi - finished farm products. The central objective of the conc ept of Dry Harvest Production Management, therefore , is the backward deployment and integration of technologies for the abundant wealth in agriculture between the rural and urban economies . This build s capacity and empowerment that foster industrialization in food production . This is one solution that can sustain moving the national and local economies to self - sufficiency and self - reliant from the grassroots unstoppably . 1.2 MONEY AND ENTERPRENUER In Nigeria, most enterprises are usually informal and self - e mployed with fewer workers requiring micro - credit to operate as sole proprietors without formal registration. Most are regarded as business undertakings of the poor. Incidentally, the p oor have become target s in development programmes , because we can learn from money - managing efforts of the poor and use that learning to design new and better ways of bringing capacity management services to the

A poor person in Nigeria is described as a person earning below the national minimum wage or not more than twice of per capital income, whichever is higher (CBN). Hence the level of poverty of the poor is highly influenced by the national economic management. 1.3 THE MICRO ENTERPRISE Self - employment requires assets in the form of human capital (education, experience, and entrepreneurship), financial capital (loans or savings), and social capital (networks and personal support). Proper Micro enterprise capacity building and management would help people of modest means to start, strengthen or expand very small companies. Self - employment requires a wide range of skills, attitudes, and habits. The people most likely to succeed are the elderly educated with experience in self - employment or in wage jobs in the same field , who are cash and social socially prudent . 1.4 TRAINING AND PLANNING CAPACITY Training is very vital in sustainable micro factory asset building. Training aims to equip micro enterprise owners with the human capital needed to handle the technology and compete in the marketplace through: 1. Advice about the risks of micro enterprises and alternatives. 2. Help with business plans . 3. General skills in accounting, planning, and pricing 4. Assistance with legal compliance and licensing for specific businesses.
pages.14: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 3 5. Consulting services and technical assistance on an on - going, on - call basis. A critical element of self - employment training is to help clients understand whether they are suited as entrepreneurs. Good training helps the poor to assess their assets , get more education, an d to search for skills in vocational job s , and then attempt self - employment. For one thing, planning forces owners to ask some tough questions: 1. Does the idea make sense in business terms? 2. How long will it take to break even, and how will I get by then? 3. Have I confused the enjoyment of supply with the existence of demand? 4. If I make it, will they come? That is, customers being the king. Most owners start making a product because they like it rather than because it has a profitable market. Business plan gr e atly serves three good purposes: 1. For micro enterprise management that is based on loans, the business plan screens out the highest - risk borrowers - no plan, no loan. 2. For management that does not make loans, the business plan prepares borrowers to approach banks or other lenders. 3. Finally, the plan serves as a “final exam” and to track effort toward self - employment. Sector - specific training makes sense in some fields such as food service that not only have many micro enterprises -

Products (loans) and the market (the poor) fall within the purview of microfinance, but they are more its origins than its present and future. The microfinance industry has developed from a history of micro credit programmes. Today, it has grown to cover a broader range of products and services, from credit and savings to insurance and mo ney transfers. Today, the general term of microfinance is the provision of financial services to those excluded from the formal financial system. The services noted here hint at the potential breadth of 'micro financial' services. Reaching "those excluded from formal financial services" means an expanding focus for microfinance. Systems of exclusion are based not just on lack of wealth, but also on social, cultural and gender barriers to financial services. Effective microfinance is positioned to overcome a variety of access barriers to a wide range of financial services for the many different customers who are excluded from the formal financial system. The future of micro and small businesses is the future of micro finance. Recent research highlights the various levels of poverty of the entrepreneurial groups reached by microfinance services. This research recognizes that poor and low - income people slip from one poverty category to another as opportunities and risks change . This is because microfinance has c ome to the rescue of many micro investors
pages.16: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 5 by granting loans without the usual stringent requirements of universal banks. The micro financial institutions have proved to be a bailout to revive ailing micro sector particularly in Nigeria. Many have had their entrepreneurial skills upgraded and are now better able to manage their investment better. However, a shift from the concept of ‘credit need’ to ‘repayment capacity’ limits risk to MFIs and lowers unbearable debt burdens for their poor clients. 1.6 MICRO LOANS Lack of access to capital is the greatest single barrier to starting businesses, and capital is an input even more important than general business training. There is a strong link between business start - up and owner’s net worth. Banks require signals of creditworthiness that micro enterprises often cannot offer real estate for collateral, an unblemished credit record, and a wage job with enough steady income to make monthly payments. Unlike banks, micro enterprise management often uses joint - liability groups to control risk. Managers that lend to individuals also do consider non - standard signals of creditworthiness that banks ignore, such as a record of on - time payments for rent and utilities, regular remittances to relatives abroad, and/or completion of a micro enterprise training course or business plan. A few banks work in partnership with micro enterprise managers to make loans to unemployed “graduates” based on their business plans. This goes to confirm that micro loans are good business. However, a “ score point” for the SMEDAN Act in Nigeria, banks until recent times does not seem to have found a profitable niche in micro enterprises. In fact, rather than making loans themselves, some banks score Credit Risk

Conventional banks only spoke of “micro credit”. The new shift through government policy and empowerment programmes shows the awareness that, for micro enterprises, savings matter much if not more as loans. Most new ventures do not use much debt at start - up. In the Nigeria nascent democratic social and economic development, start - ups financial capital most common sources are not bank loans but rather owner’s savings or informal loans from friends or relatives. Formal loans are little used in financing business start - ups. Micro enterprises are limited less by low debt than by low savings because lenders require collateral, low savings lead to low access to loans. Savings have several advantages over loans. Savings pay interest, but loans cost interest, and loans are tied to specific purchases and cannot pay for research during the planning stage or during the years of gestation required of most small ventures. A micro enterprise invests a lot of “pre - venture capital” long before it gets in the sights of a bank. Even if established, successful micro enterprises do not provide monthly payment and need savings on income and expenses. Without a reserve of savings, a new small business will fold before the start. 1.8 SOCIAL SUPPORT In addition to human capital and financial capital, self - employment requires social capital. Business happens not only in the marketplace but also in the social arena, and the
pages.18: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 7 self - employed must rely on their personal networks for contacts and information and on their families for emotional support and physical sustenance. Self - employment is difficult for anyone, and micro enterprises are not a panacea for disadvantaged groups . “Business failure and self - employment exit rates are high er a mong people who choose self - employment without appropriate education, skills, and financial resources. In the long term , the best way to promote self - employment for disadvantaged groups is through improved educational opportunities. Self - employment is not the same as entrepreneurship, and many people of modest means enter micro enterprise not because they are risk - takers who want to get rich through “creativity” but because they cannot find a g ood wage job and so need a stop - gap measure as they tread until something better comes along. To increase the chances that slow - growing and or no - growing will transform into the fast - growing and subsequent micro economic growth in Nigeria . Micro enterprise support must offer “self - esteem training” to buttress resilience that ins pire “entrepreneurial spirits. Even for motivated low - income, micro enterprise training does not generally increase living standards in the short run although it does make owners fe el better. Sorting: The freshly harvested tubers are sorted mainly by visual assessment. Defective tubers and extr aneous matters are separated and discarded. 2. Weighing: The sorted tubers are weighed with industrial weighing scale. The total weight of the input (raw material) can be recorded.
pages.47: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 36 3. Peeling: The separation of inedible peels from the edible portion of the tubers is accomplished by manual peeling. The peels can be utilized for poultry feed formulation or serve as source of fuel for industrial plants. 4. Washing: The peeled roots are thoroughly washed with hygienically clean water to remove both physical and biologi cal contaminants, which can adversely affect the quality of the finished product. In addition, free starch is released by the cutting action of the peeling knife or brushing during harvesting. Washing can be accomplished manually or mechanically (using a drum washer). 5. Grating: After weighing (to calculate the peeling loss) the peeled tubers are subjected to the size reduction unit operation called grating. Ideally, a hammer mill is used to produce a smooth mash, which would result in a superior quality prod uct with higher yield.
pages.48: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 37 6. Fermentation: The mash is aerobically fermented in a non - corrosive container for a very short period, (2hrs). From zero hours to the end of the period, the mash is intermittently and vigorously stirred manually or mechanically. This ensures intimate contact of the enzyme (endogenous) with hydrolysis of the cyanogenic complex and maximum liberation of the severed hydrogen cyanide. The process is termed detoxification. 7. Dewatering: Immediately after the fermentation period, the mash deto xified is dewatered from about 75% moisture content to less than 50%. Several systems are available such as of those in use at FIIRO manual screw press, hydraulic press and basket centrifuge. The resultant product is termed “CAKE” 8. Granulating : The semi - solid wet “cake” is mechanically size – reduced using a hammer mill granulator. Granulation produces fine granules with greater surface - area than cake. 9. Dehydration: Dehydration (or drying) of the fine granules is accomplished using a mechanical (rotary hot ai r) dryer rather than sun drying. Owing to increase in the surface area of the granules the drying is much faster. Mechanical drying ensures improved and consistent product quality. The flash dryer is equally good equipment for drying cassava flour. The moisture content of the product is about 8 - 10%. 10. Milling: The dried product is milled with a hammer mill to produce a fine powder. 11. Sieving: The powder is sieved to separate the fibre from the required fine flour (a creamy - white product).
pages.49: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 38 12. pages.51: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 40 3.8 G ARRI PRODUCTION Gari is creamy - white, granular flour with a slightly fermented flavor and a slightly sour taste made from fermented, gelatinized fresh cassava tubers. Gari is widely known in Nigeria and other West African countries. It is commonly consumed either by being soaked in cold water with sugar, coconut, roasted ground nuts , dry fish, or boiled cowpea as complements or as a paste made with hot water and eaten with vegetable sauce. When properly stored, it has a shelf - life of six months or more. Raw material Fresh cassava should be free from microbial or insect damage and without serious bruising or cuts. It should be processed within two days of harvest to prevent deterioration and loss of quality in gari . Hygiene Fresh cassava is a moist, low - acid food that is susceptible
pages.52: Dry Harvest Agricultural Entrepreneurship 41 to bacterial and fungal growth. Hygienic practices, especially in the early stages of processing, should ensure minimal contamination. All waste materials from the process should be removed from the site as they are produced to avoid the risk of cross - contamination. Process control Washing should be carried out thoroughly to avoid contamination of the final product with peel, sand, and so on. Fermentation must be properly controlled, as a period too short will result in incomplete detoxification and a blend product. Too long a period will give the product a strong sour taste. Both over - and under fermentation also badly affect the texture of the final gari . If too much liquid is pressed from the grated cassava, the gelatinization of starch during subsequent roasting is affected and the product is whiter. If sufficient liquid is not removed, however, the formation of granules during roasting is affected and the dough is more likely to form into lumps. The ideal moisture content is 47 - 50%, and experienced gari producers assess this visually. Sieving is important to obtain a high - quality product, free of fibrous contaminants and with similar - sized granules. The granules must be roasted to about 80ºC/175 ºF to achieve partial gelatinization of the starch. If lower temperatures are used, the product simply dries and produces a dry white powder. Too high a temperature wi ll cause charring of the product and make it stick to the roasting pan.

The method of production of lafun is different from that of fufu . In the traditional preparation, f resh cassava roots are cut into chunks and steeped for 3 - 4 days or until the roots become soft. The fermented roots are broken up into small pieces, and sun dried on mats, flat rocks, cement floors, or the roofs of houses.
